ai-tech-law/california/deepfake-laws.summary: California regulates deepfakes through several targeted laws rather than one general ban on AI-generated media: its rules address sexually explicit depictions, certain criminal distributions, performers’ digital-replica contracts, and deceased personalities’ publicity rights. Whether a particular use is unlawful depends on the statute’s requirements, including consent, knowledge, harm, contractual representation, or an applicable expressive-use exception; labeling content as AI-generated does not automatically make it lawful.

sections.heading: Sexually explicit deepfakes: civil and criminal rules

facts.label: Civil claims against creators
facts.value: A depicted individual can bring a civil action against someone who creates and intentionally discloses sexually explicit material when that person knows or reasonably should know the individual did not consent to its creation or disclosure. The statute covers qualifying material altered through digitization — California Civil Code § 1708.86.

facts.label: Claims against distributors
facts.value: The civil law also reaches someone who intentionally discloses qualifying material that the person did not create, with knowledge that the depicted individual did not consent to its creation — California Civil Code § 1708.86.

facts.label: Criminal liability
facts.value: California’s disorderly-conduct statute includes intentional distribution of qualifying intimate images created or altered through digitization. Liability requires the statutory conditions, including the required knowledge concerning serious emotional distress and that the depicted person actually suffer that distress; not every AI-generated image satisfies those elements — California Penal Code § 647(j)(4).

sections.heading: Protections and remedies by type of use

rows: Civil remedies include actual damages or statutory damages, plus other available relief.
The statutory range is $1,500–$30,000; the statute permits up to $150,000 for conduct committed with malice.
Distribution of covered digitized intimate images can constitute misdemeanor disorderly conduct.
Certain provisions authorizing replacement of personal services with digital replicas are unenforceable when the statute’s conditions are met.
Unauthorized production, distribution, or availability of qualifying replicas in expressive audiovisual works or sound recordings can create civil liability, subject to exceptions.

facts.label: Contract safeguards
facts.value: The contract rule concerns a digital replica used instead of work the individual otherwise would have performed personally. Its conditions include an insufficiently specific description of intended uses and the absence of qualifying legal or labor-union representation. It does not automatically invalidate every agreement involving AI — California Labor Code § 927.

facts.label: Postmortem protection
facts.value: California’s deceased-personality statute generally protects covered rights for 70 years after death. Its digital-replica provisions contain exceptions, including specified news, public-affairs, documentary, historical, commentary, criticism, satire, and parody uses, subject to statutory conditions — California Civil Code § 3344.1.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in California
bullets: California Superior Courts hear state-law civil claims under Civil Code §§ 1708.86 and 3344.1. These are civil lawsuits, distinct from criminal complaints.
Local police departments and county sheriffs receive reports of suspected criminal distribution under Penal Code § 647(j)(4). Prosecutors, rather than private complainants, bring criminal charges.
Disputes about digital-replica contract enforceability involve Labor Code § 927; the statute does not create a general licensing or approval system for AI-generated performances.

sections.heading: Common questions in California
bullets: Does an AI disclaimer eliminate liability? No. Civil Code § 1708.86 expressly provides that a disclaimer identifying unauthorized sexually explicit material does not itself defeat liability.
Must the depicted person be famous? No. The sexually explicit deepfake civil statute protects qualifying depicted individuals, not just celebrities.
Is every digital-replica contract unenforceable? No. Labor Code § 927 applies only when its specified conditions are satisfied.
Are satire and documentaries always prohibited? No. Civil Code § 3344.1 includes expressive-use exceptions, but their statutory conditions matter.

ai-tech-law/georgia/right-to-repair.summary: In Georgia, repair disputes involving AI-enabled devices, connected appliances, and other consumer technology can involve sales warranties, consumer-protection law, federal warranty restrictions, and rules governing software access. These protections are not interchangeable: a warranty claim concerns the seller’s or warrantor’s obligations, while access to diagnostic software, cloud services, source code, or replacement components presents separate questions that depend on the product, contract, and applicable law.

facts.label: Merchantability
facts.value: Unless excluded or modified, a merchant selling goods of that kind provides an implied warranty of merchantability. Goods must be fit for their ordinary purposes. This rule concerns the goods’ condition and performance, not a general obligation to publish repair instructions or AI source code. — O.C.G.A. § 11-2-314.

facts.label: Warranty exclusions
facts.value: A written exclusion of merchantability must mention merchantability and be conspicuous. Georgia law also recognizes exclusions using expressions such as “as is,” subject to statutory requirements and other applicable law. Federal consumer-warranty law can limit exclusions where a written warranty or qualifying service contract exists. — O.C.G.A. § 11-2-316; 15 U.S.C. § 2308.

facts.label: Misleading repair representations
facts.value: Georgia’s Fair Business Practices Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in consumer transactions and consumer trade or commerce. False representations about a product’s characteristics, benefits, or warranty rights can implicate the Act; a repair disagreement alone does not establish deception. — O.C.G.A. § 10-1-393.

rows: A consumer-product warrantor generally cannot condition coverage on branded parts or services unless provided without charge or covered by an FTC waiver.
Federal warranty rules permit exclusion of damage caused by unauthorized parts or service; independent service does not automatically eliminate all coverage.
Georgia generally allows four years after accrual. An original agreement may reduce this to at least one year, but cannot extend it.
Ordinarily, breach occurs upon tender of delivery, even without knowledge of the defect. An explicit future-performance warranty can change the accrual rule.
Federal copyright law separately restricts circumvention of access controls. Statutory and regulatory exemptions are limited, not blanket repair permissions.

facts.label: Goods versus services
facts.value: Georgia’s Uniform Commercial Code sales provisions apply to transactions in goods. A cloud subscription or AI service is not automatically governed by the same rules as the physical device it supports. — O.C.G.A. §§ 11-2-102, 11-2-105.

facts.label: Repair does not authorize every access method
facts.value: Georgia’s Computer Systems Protection Act defines offenses involving unauthorized computer use, including computer theft and computer trespass. The statutory elements matter; a repair purpose does not itself supply permission to access another party’s systems. — O.C.G.A. §§ 16-9-92, 16-9-93.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Georgia
bullets: The Georgia Attorney General’s Consumer Protection Division accepts complaints involving allegedly unfair or deceptive business practices. It does not serve as the consumer’s private lawyer.

Georgia magistrate courts hear qualifying civil claims involving $15,000 or less, subject to jurisdictional exceptions. Larger claims may fall within state or superior court jurisdiction. — O.C.G.A. § 15-10-2.

A private Fair Business Practices Act damages claim generally requires a written demand delivered at least 30 days before filing. Its limitation period is generally two years. — O.C.G.A. §§ 10-1-399(b), 10-1-401.

sections.heading: Common questions in Georgia
bullets: Does a warranty require disclosure of AI source code? Not by itself; warranty coverage and software-access rights are separate.
Does independent repair automatically void a warranty? No. Federal law restricts branded-service conditions, while allowing exclusions for damage caused by unauthorized service.
Is every failed repair consumer fraud? No. Defective performance and an unfair or deceptive practice are different legal questions.
Do repair rights guarantee continued cloud access? The cited warranty provisions do not establish a blanket entitlement to continued cloud or AI services.

ai-tech-law/nevada/data-privacy-rights.summary: Nevada gives consumers a limited right to stop certain sales of personal information by covered website operators and data brokers, rather than a general right to control every use of their data. Nevada also separately protects consumer health data outside traditional medical settings, including some information inferred through algorithms. These laws can apply to AI businesses, but they do not create a general right to explanations of AI decisions or deletion of all personal information.

sections.heading: Online privacy rights and their limits

facts.label: Who and what are covered
facts.value: Nevada’s online privacy provisions cover qualifying commercial website and online-service operators and separately regulate data brokers. Covered information includes specified identifiers, such as names, email addresses and telephone numbers, collected and maintained in the circumstances defined by the law. Exemptions limit coverage. — NRS Chapter 603A, online privacy provisions.

facts.label: Privacy notices
facts.value: Covered operators must make a privacy notice available identifying categories of information collected and categories of third parties with whom it may be shared. The notice must also address any available review-and-change process and how material notice changes are communicated. This disclosure requirement does not itself establish a general correction right. — NRS Chapter 603A, online privacy provisions.

facts.label: Narrow meaning of sale
facts.value: The online privacy law’s sale definition requires monetary consideration and contains exclusions. Consequently, an opt-out does not prohibit every disclosure, advertising arrangement or use of information for AI development. — NRS Chapter 603A, online privacy provisions.

rows: Consumers may submit verified requests directing covered operators or data brokers not to sell covered information about them.
A response is due within 60 days after receipt of a verified request.
An additional 30 days is permitted when reasonably necessary, with notice to the consumer.
The Attorney General may seek an injunction or a civil penalty of up to $5,000 for each violation.
These online privacy provisions do not establish a private right of action against an operator or data broker.

sections.heading: Consumer health data and AI inferences

facts.label: Separate health-data protections
facts.value: Nevada’s consumer health data law establishes rights concerning access, deletion and consent withdrawal for covered data. It generally requires consent for collection and sharing, subject to exceptions, and separate written authorization for sale. Its coverage and exemptions differ from the online sale-opt-out rules. — Nevada SB 370 (2023), enacted in NRS Chapter 603A.

facts.label: Inferred health information
facts.value: Consumer health data can include information derived or extrapolated from nonhealth information through algorithms or machine learning when used to associate a consumer with protected health information. An AI-generated health inference can therefore fall within the law even when its underlying inputs were not medical records. — Nevada SB 370 (2023).

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Nevada
bullets: Covered operators and data brokers must establish a designated request address for verified sale-opt-out requests; this may be an email address, toll-free telephone number or website. — NRS Chapter 603A.

The Nevada Attorney General’s Bureau of Consumer Protection receives consumer complaints. The Attorney General enforces Nevada’s online privacy and consumer health data provisions. — NRS Chapter 603A.

sections.heading: Common questions in Nevada
bullets: Can every Nevada resident demand deletion of every company record? No. The online privacy provisions do not provide a general deletion right; the separate consumer health data law provides a more specific deletion right.
Does opting out stop all AI training? No. The online sale opt-out is not a general prohibition on internal data processing or model training.
Are health apps automatically exempt because HIPAA exists? No. Nevada’s consumer health data protections can reach data outside HIPAA, subject to statutory coverage and exemptions.
Can an algorithm’s prediction count as health data? Yes, qualifying inferred or extrapolated information can fall within Nevada’s consumer health data definition.

ai-tech-law/minnesota/right-to-repair.summary: Minnesota’s Digital Fair Repair Act requires manufacturers of covered digital electronic equipment to make repair documentation, parts, and tools available to equipment owners and independent repair providers on fair and reasonable terms. The law took effect July 1, 2024, and generally applies to covered equipment first sold on or after July 1, 2021, subject to statutory exclusions. It addresses access to repair resources, including certain software tools, rather than creating a general right to inspect or modify an AI model.

facts.label: Governing law
facts.value: Minnesota’s Digital Fair Repair Act is codified at Minnesota Statutes section 325E.72. It establishes obligations for original equipment manufacturers concerning diagnosis, maintenance, and repair of covered digital electronic equipment. — Minn. Stat. § 325E.72

facts.label: Covered technology
facts.value: Digital electronic equipment generally means a product that depends for its functioning, in whole or in part, on digital electronics embedded in or attached to it. Parts for that equipment are included within the statutory definition. — Minn. Stat. § 325E.72

facts.label: Who receives access
facts.value: The statute requires qualifying repair resources to be made available to equipment owners and independent repair providers, not only to manufacturer-authorized repair businesses. The obligation concerns equipment and parts sold or used in Minnesota. — Minn. Stat. § 325E.72

rows: Covered repair documentation must be available on fair and reasonable terms.
The access requirement includes covered parts, subject to statutory availability limitations.
Required tools include applicable embedded software, firmware, and other repair software tools.
The law addresses access to documentation, tools, and parts needed to disable and reset an electronic security lock or security-related function during diagnosis, maintenance, or repair.
The statute does not require trade-secret disclosure except as necessary to provide required documentation, parts, and tools on fair and reasonable terms.

sections.heading: Limits for AI-enabled devices and other equipment

facts.label: AI is not a separate coverage category
facts.value: Coverage turns on the equipment and statutory requirements, not simply whether a product uses artificial intelligence. Section 325E.72 does not establish a separate entitlement to AI training data or general model transparency. — Minn. Stat. § 325E.72

facts.label: Excluded equipment
facts.value: The statute contains exclusions involving motor vehicles, medical devices, agricultural equipment, and video game consoles. Its repair-access obligations therefore do not apply uniformly to every product containing electronics. — Minn. Stat. § 325E.72

facts.label: Repair versus modification
facts.value: The law does not require manufacturers to make available special documentation, tools, or parts that would disable or override antitheft security measures without the owner’s authorization. — Minn. Stat. § 325E.72

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Minnesota
bullets: Minnesota Attorney General’s Office: Consumer complaints concerning manufacturer compliance fall within the office’s consumer-protection role. The Digital Fair Repair Act expressly provides for attorney-general enforcement under Minnesota Statutes section 8.31. — Minn. Stat. § 325E.72.

Minnesota district courts: Attorney-general enforcement under section 8.31 can include court proceedings seeking injunctions and other statutory relief. An agency complaint is not itself a court judgment establishing a violation. — Minn. Stat. § 8.31.

sections.heading: Common questions in Minnesota
bullets: Does Minnesota require every repair to be free? No. The statute requires fair and reasonable access terms; it does not make all parts, tools, and repair labor free. — Minn. Stat. § 325E.72.
Does an independent repair shop qualify for access? Yes, independent repair providers are expressly included in the access requirement for covered equipment. — Minn. Stat. § 325E.72.
Does the law cover older products? Its applicability provision generally reaches covered equipment first sold on or after July 1, 2021. — Minn. Stat. § 325E.72.

Does an AI feature automatically create a right to the model’s source code? No. The law establishes repair-resource access requirements, not an unrestricted source-code disclosure right. — Minn. Stat. § 325E.72.

ai-tech-law/new-mexico/terms-of-service-.summary: In New Mexico, an AI service’s terms of service can form an enforceable contract electronically, but electronic presentation alone does not establish agreement or make every clause enforceable. The Uniform Electronic Transactions Act recognizes electronic records, signatures, and automated contracting, while ordinary contract defenses, the Uniform Arbitration Act, and the Unfair Practices Act remain relevant to subscription charges, arbitration provisions, liability limits, and representations about what an AI product can do.

facts.label: Electronic format
facts.value: A record or signature cannot be denied legal effect solely because it is electronic. Likewise, a contract cannot be denied enforceability solely because an electronic record was used in its formation. These rules remove a format barrier; they do not automatically validate every provision in an AI provider’s terms. — NMSA 1978, § 14-16-7.

facts.label: Agreement to transact electronically
facts.value: The Uniform Electronic Transactions Act applies to transactions between parties that have agreed to conduct them electronically. Whether they agreed is determined from the context and surrounding circumstances, including their conduct. — NMSA 1978, § 14-16-5(B).

facts.label: Attributing acceptance
facts.value: An electronic record or signature is attributable to a person if it was that person’s act. Attribution may be shown in any manner, and its legal effect depends on the context and circumstances surrounding its creation, execution, or adoption. — NMSA 1978, § 14-16-9.

sections.heading: Rules affecting common AI service provisions

rows: Electronic agents can form contracts even when no individual reviews their actions or the resulting terms.
An arbitration agreement contained in a record is generally enforceable, subject to grounds available for revoking a contract.
The court decides whether an arbitration agreement exists and whether a controversy is subject to it.
Unfair or deceptive trade practices and unconscionable trade practices in trade or commerce are unlawful.
For qualifying losses under the Unfair Practices Act, recovery is actual damages or $100, whichever is greater; willful violations can support an increase.

facts.label: AI marketing representations
facts.value: The Unfair Practices Act addresses qualifying false or misleading representations made in connection with selling goods or services. Claims about an AI service’s characteristics, uses, benefits, or quality can implicate these statutory categories; coverage depends on the statutory elements and facts. — NMSA 1978, § 57-12-2(D).

facts.label: Attorney fees
facts.value: The court must award attorney fees and costs to a complaining party who prevails under the Unfair Practices Act. A defending party receives fees and costs when the court finds that the claimant brought a groundless action. — NMSA 1978, § 57-12-10(C).

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in New Mexico
bullets: The New Mexico Department of Justice receives consumer complaints involving businesses and potentially unfair or deceptive practices.
New Mexico district courts hear civil contract disputes. The Unfair Practices Act expressly authorizes district-court actions for injunctive relief under its terms. — NMSA 1978, § 57-12-10(A).

sections.heading: Common questions in New Mexico
bullets: Are online terms automatically binding? No. Electronic form is legally recognized, but agreement and other contract requirements still matter.
Can software form a contract without human review? Yes. Section 14-16-14 expressly recognizes certain contracts formed through electronic agents.
Does an arbitration clause always control? No. Section 44-7A-7 preserves contract-revocation grounds and assigns specified threshold questions to courts.
Does inaccurate AI output automatically establish consumer fraud? No. A claim must satisfy the applicable statutory elements; an incorrect output alone does not establish them.

ai-tech-law/illinois/online-defamation.summary: Illinois defamation law can apply to false factual claims published online, including claims conveyed through AI-generated text, images, audio, or video, when the ordinary requirements for liability are met. Libel and slander claims generally have a one-year filing deadline, and Illinois follows a single-publication rule that matters when material remains available online. Liability depends on factors including defamatory meaning, identification, publication, fault, privileges, and whether damages must be proved.

facts.label: Basic claim
facts.value: A plaintiff generally must establish a false statement about the plaintiff, an unprivileged publication to a third party, and resulting damages. Constitutional fault requirements also apply; public officials and public figures generally must prove knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for truth. — Green v. Rogers, 234 Ill. 2d 478 (2009); New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, 376 U.S. 254 (1964).

facts.label: One-year deadline
facts.value: Illinois requires actions for slander and libel to be commenced within one year after the cause of action accrues. Continued online availability does not itself create a fresh deadline each day. — 735 ILCS 5/13-201; Pippen v. NBCUniversal Media, LLC, 734 F.3d 610 (7th Cir. 2013).

facts.label: Single publication
facts.value: The Uniform Single Publication Act limits claims arising from a single publication or broadcast to one cause of action. A genuinely separate republication can present a different issue from leaving an existing webpage accessible. — 740 ILCS 165/1; Pippen v. NBCUniversal Media, LLC, 734 F.3d 610 (7th Cir. 2013).

facts.label: AI-generated material
facts.value: An AI label does not alone determine liability. Illinois evaluates whether the communication, read in context, reasonably conveys a defamatory factual assertion about an identifiable plaintiff; obvious parody and nonfactual opinion receive different treatment. — Solaia Technology, LLC v. Specialty Publishing Co., 221 Ill. 2d 558 (2006).

sections.heading: How common online scenarios are treated

rows: Words imputing commission of a crime are a recognized defamation-per-se category, subject to context and the innocent-construction rule. — Green v. Rogers, 234 Ill. 2d 478 (2009).
Certain statements prejudicing someone in a profession or trade, or imputing inability or lack of integrity in employment duties, qualify as defamation per se. — Green v. Rogers.
Calling something an opinion is not decisive. Courts consider whether it conveys a provably false factual assertion in context. — Solaia Technology, 221 Ill. 2d 558.

Illinois Supreme Court Rule 224 permits a verified petition for discovery to identify potential defendants. A defamation petition must satisfy substantive pleading requirements. — Hadley v. Doe, 2015 IL 118000.

Federal Section 230 generally prevents treating an interactive computer service provider or user as the publisher of information supplied by another information content provider; this is not blanket protection for creating defamatory content. — 47 U.S.C. § 230(c)(1), (f)(3).

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Illinois
bullets: Illinois circuit courts hear state-law civil defamation cases. Venue generally lies where a properly joined defendant resides or where the transaction, or part of it, occurred, subject to statutory exceptions. — 735 ILCS 5/2-101.
Rule 224 identification proceedings are filed in circuit court and are limited to discovery needed to identify responsible persons or entities. — Illinois Supreme Court Rule 224.
The Illinois Attorney General's consumer-complaint process is not a substitute for a civil defamation lawsuit. Private defamation damages are determined through court proceedings.

sections.heading: Common questions in Illinois
bullets: Does every damaging statement qualify? No. Substantial truth defeats a defamation claim, and context can make a statement nonactionable. — Solaia Technology.
Must financial loss always be proved? No. Defamation per se permits presumed damages under Illinois law, subject to applicable constitutional restrictions. — Green v. Rogers.
Does an old post become newly actionable whenever someone reads it? Generally no; continued access alone does not restart the limitations period. — Pippen.
Can an anonymous poster be identified through court proceedings? Potentially, through a properly supported Rule 224 petition; anonymity alone does not prevent discovery. — Hadley v. Doe.

ai-tech-law/kentucky/social-media-legal-.summary: Kentucky social media disputes can involve consumer protection, privacy, defamation, and criminal laws, whether content is created by a person or generated using AI. The Kentucky Consumer Data Protection Act took effect January 1, 2026, giving qualifying consumers rights against covered businesses, while existing laws address deceptive commercial practices and harassing communications. Not every platform or AI service falls within the privacy act, and its enforcement belongs to the attorney general rather than private plaintiffs.

sections.heading: Kentucky privacy rights for social media and AI services

facts.label: Coverage thresholds
facts.value: The Kentucky Consumer Data Protection Act covers businesses operating in Kentucky or targeting Kentucky residents that control or process at least 100,000 consumers’ personal data, or at least 25,000 consumers’ data while deriving over 50% of gross revenue from personal-data sales. Statutory exemptions also apply. — Kentucky Consumer Data Protection Act, 2024 HB 15.

facts.label: Who qualifies as a consumer
facts.value: A consumer is a Kentucky resident acting in an individual or household context. People acting in commercial or employment contexts are excluded from that definition. — Kentucky Consumer Data Protection Act, 2024 HB 15.

facts.label: Rights and response deadline
facts.value: Covered consumers have rights to access, correct, delete, and obtain copies of qualifying personal data, and to opt out of targeted advertising, data sales, and certain profiling. Controllers generally must respond within 45 days; a further 45-day extension is permitted when reasonably necessary, with notice. — Kentucky Consumer Data Protection Act, 2024 HB 15.

facts.label: AI-related limits
facts.value: The profiling opt-out concerns solely automated decisions producing legal or similarly significant effects. It is not a general right to reject every AI-generated recommendation or social media ranking. — Kentucky Consumer Data Protection Act, 2024 HB 15.

sections.heading: Other Kentucky laws affecting online conduct

rows: Unfair, false, misleading, or deceptive practices in trade or commerce are unlawful; the rule is not limited to offline advertising.
Qualifying purchasers of goods or services primarily for personal, family, or household use may seek relief for ascertainable losses caused by unlawful practices.
Communications made with the required intent and in a manner causing annoyance or alarm can constitute harassing communications. The offense is a Class B misdemeanor.
Kentucky generally requires libel or slander actions to be commenced within one year after the cause of action accrues.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Kentucky
bullets: The Kentucky Attorney General’s Office handles consumer-protection complaints involving deceptive commercial practices and has exclusive enforcement authority under the Kentucky Consumer Data Protection Act.

Kentucky circuit courts have general jurisdiction over civil disputes unless jurisdiction is assigned elsewhere. District courts handle qualifying civil cases within their statutory jurisdiction. The correct court depends on the claim and relief sought. — Kentucky Constitution § 112; KRS 24A.120.

Local police departments and county sheriffs receive reports of potentially criminal online conduct. Whether a message satisfies a criminal statute depends on its content, context, and the required intent.

sections.heading: Common questions in Kentucky
bullets: Can I sue under Kentucky’s data privacy act? The act does not create a private right of action. Attorney general enforcement is separate from any claim available under another law.
Does AI-generated advertising escape consumer-protection law? No. KRS 367.170 addresses deceptive commercial practices without an exemption merely because advertising was generated using AI.
Is every offensive post criminal harassment? No. KRS 525.080 requires statutory elements, including the required intent; offensiveness alone does not establish the offense.
Does the privacy act cover employee social media data? Its consumer definition excludes people acting in an employment context. That exclusion does not determine whether other laws apply.

ai-tech-law/louisiana/right-to-repair.summary: In Louisiana, disputes over repairing AI-enabled devices can involve the Civil Code’s warranty against hidden defects, written product warranties, and consumer-protection law. Those protections can support repair, a price reduction, or cancellation of a sale in qualifying cases, but they do not automatically require manufacturers to release source code, diagnostic software, or proprietary repair tools. Federal warranty and copyright rules also affect what manufacturers and independent repairers may do.

facts.label: Hidden defects
facts.value: Louisiana calls its warranty against hidden defects “redhibition.” A defect can justify undoing a sale if it makes the product useless or so inconvenient that the buyer would not have purchased it. A less serious defect can support a price reduction. Whether an AI-related malfunction qualifies depends on the facts. — Louisiana Civil Code art. 2520

facts.label: Notice and opportunity to repair
facts.value: The buyer generally must notify the seller of a redhibitory defect in time to allow repairs. Failure to notify reduces recovery to the extent timely notice would have avoided damage; notice is unnecessary when the seller actually knew of the defect. — Louisiana Civil Code art. 2522

facts.label: Seller’s knowledge matters
facts.value: A seller who did not know of the defect generally must repair, remedy, or correct it before facing the article’s refund obligations. A seller who knew of the defect and failed to disclose it can also owe damages and reasonable attorney fees; a manufacturer is deemed to know its product’s redhibitory defects. — Louisiana Civil Code arts. 2531 and 2545

rows: Redhibition concerns defects in the thing sold, not an automatic entitlement to repair information.
Covered warranties generally cannot require identified branded parts or service unless supplied free or an FTC waiver applies.
Damage caused by an independent repair
Warranty coverage may be denied for damage caused by improper repairs or replacement parts.
Unfair or deceptive trade practices are unlawful; a repair disagreement alone does not establish a violation.

sections.heading: AI software, access controls, and repair

facts.label: Repair rights are not source-code rights
facts.value: The cited Louisiana redhibition provisions establish sale-related remedies, not a general obligation to publish source code, model weights, passwords, or diagnostic tools. — Louisiana Civil Code arts. 2520 and 2531

facts.label: Digital locks
facts.value: Federal copyright law generally prohibits circumventing technological measures controlling access to copyrighted works. Regulatory exemptions are limited; permission to circumvent for a qualifying purpose does not itself require a manufacturer to provide tools or credentials. — 17 U.S.C. § 1201(a)

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Louisiana
bullets: The Louisiana Department of Justice, Office of the Attorney General, Consumer Protection Section receives consumer complaints involving businesses, including repair and warranty disputes.
The Federal Trade Commission receives reports about deceptive business practices and warranty restrictions through ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

Private redhibition and consumer-protection claims may be brought in Louisiana courts with jurisdiction. Louisiana Revised Statutes § 51:1409 authorizes a private action for qualifying ascertainable losses caused by prohibited practices. Talk to a lawyer.

sections.heading: Common questions in Louisiana
bullets: Does an AI feature eliminate Louisiana defect protections? No. Article 2520 addresses defects in things sold; applying it to a particular device or software arrangement depends on the transaction and defect.
Does independent service automatically void a warranty? No. Federal law restricts branded-service conditions in covered warranties, although repair-caused damage can be excluded.
Can a seller exclude redhibition? An exclusion must be clear, unambiguous, and brought to the buyer’s attention. Article 2548 also limits when a seller can rely on it.

Is every unsuccessful repair an unfair trade practice? No. A claim under Louisiana Revised Statutes § 51:1409 requires the statutory elements, including qualifying loss caused by a prohibited practice.

ai-tech-law/nevada/right-to-repair.summary: In Nevada, repair disputes involving AI-enabled devices can turn on warranties, sales contracts, and consumer-fraud law; those rules do not automatically require a manufacturer to disclose source code, model weights, or diagnostic tools. Nevada’s commercial code provides warranty protections for qualifying sales of goods, while federal law restricts certain warranty conditions requiring branded parts or services. Whether those protections cover a particular connected product depends on the transaction, warranty terms, and alleged defect or misrepresentation.

facts.label: Promises about repairability
facts.value: A seller’s factual promise or product description can create an express warranty when it becomes part of the basis of the bargain. Statements about replaceable components, repair access, or functionality may therefore matter; a seller’s opinion or commendation alone does not create that warranty. — NRS 104.2313

facts.label: Misleading product claims
facts.value: Nevada prohibits knowingly false representations about goods’ characteristics, uses, or benefits. A false claim about an AI-enabled device’s capabilities or repair features can implicate this rule, but the statutory requirements still must be established. — NRS 598.0915(5)

facts.label: Limits of these protections
facts.value: Warranty and deceptive-trade-practice provisions address promises, product quality, and misleading conduct. They are not a general entitlement to proprietary AI materials or unrestricted access to a manufacturer’s repair systems. — NRS 104.2313–104.2316; NRS 598.0915

rows: Unless properly excluded or modified, a merchant seller warrants that goods are fit for their ordinary purposes.
A warranty can arise when the seller knows the buyer’s particular purpose and reliance on the seller’s judgment.
Written merchantability disclaimers must mention merchantability and be conspicuous; other statutory exclusion rules also apply.
Generally four years after accrual. The original agreement may reduce this to at least one year, but cannot extend it.
A consumer-product warrantor generally cannot condition coverage on identified branded parts or services unless supplied free or an FTC waiver applies.

facts.label: Private consumer-fraud claims
facts.value: A victim of consumer fraud may bring an action under Nevada law. If the claimant prevails, available relief includes sustained damages, appropriate equitable relief, costs, and reasonable attorney’s fees. Covered consumer fraud includes deceptive trade practices identified in the statute. — NRS 41.600

facts.label: When the warranty clock starts
facts.value: A sales-warranty claim generally accrues upon tender of delivery, even without knowledge of the breach. A specific exception applies when a warranty explicitly extends to future performance and discovery must await that performance. — NRS 104.2725(2)

facts.label: Hardware versus AI services
facts.value: Nevada’s Uniform Commercial Code Article 2 applies to transactions in goods. Its application to a combined hardware, software, and cloud-service arrangement depends on how the transaction is legally classified. — NRS 104.2102

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Nevada
bullets: The Nevada Attorney General’s Bureau of Consumer Protection accepts consumer complaints, including allegations of deceptive business practices.
Nevada state courts hear private warranty and consumer-fraud lawsuits, subject to jurisdictional requirements. Justice courts handle qualifying small-claims money disputes.
The Federal Trade Commission accepts reports about potentially unlawful warranty practices. An FTC report is distinct from a private lawsuit seeking compensation.

sections.heading: Common questions in Nevada
bullets: Does an AI feature eliminate hardware warranty protections? No. Applicable sales and consumer-product warranty rules do not disappear merely because a device includes AI.
Can a warranty require only branded repairs? Federal law generally prohibits that condition, subject to the free-service and FTC-waiver exceptions.
Does a warranty guarantee access to model weights? No. The cited warranty rules do not themselves create that access right.
Does the four-year deadline always start when a defect is discovered? No. Nevada generally measures sales-warranty accrual from delivery, with a limited future-performance exception.

ai-tech-law/new-mexico/social-media-lega.summary: In New Mexico, social media disputes involving AI-generated posts, impersonation, advertising or exposed account data can implicate consumer protection, harassment, defamation and data breach laws. The applicable rules depend on the conduct: deceptive commercial claims differ from reputational injuries, threatening messages or a business’s loss of protected personal information. Using AI does not by itself establish liability; each claim or offense has statutory or court-developed requirements, and different deadlines apply to lawsuits and breach notices.

facts.label: Deceptive commercial content
facts.value: The Unfair Practices Act covers specified false or misleading representations knowingly made in connection with selling, leasing, renting or loaning goods or services, or extending credit or collecting debts, in the regular course of trade or commerce. Commercial social media content can fall within these rules; not every inaccurate personal post does. — NMSA 1978, § 57-12-2(D)

facts.label: Private consumer remedies
facts.value: A person suffering a qualifying loss of money or property from an unlawful practice may recover actual damages or $100, whichever is greater. For a willful violation, the court may award up to three times actual damages or $300, whichever is greater. The statute also provides attorney fees and costs for a prevailing claimant. — NMSA 1978, § 57-12-10(B), (C)

facts.label: Harassment
facts.value: Harassment is a misdemeanor. It requires knowingly pursuing a pattern of conduct intended to annoy, seriously alarm or terrorize another person, serving no lawful purpose, and conduct that would cause a reasonable person substantial emotional distress. Offensive online speech alone does not establish all these elements. — NMSA 1978, § 30-3A-2

sections.heading: How common social media issues are classified

rows: The commercial representation and statutory elements matter, not simply whether AI generated the words.
The offense requires a qualifying pattern and substantial emotional distress under a reasonable-person standard.
New Mexico generally provides a three-year limitations period for injury to reputation.
Business exposure of covered personal data
Coverage depends on statutory definitions and exceptions, rather than every disclosure of online information.

facts.label: Notice to affected residents
facts.value: A covered owner or licensee of computerized personal identifying information must notify affected New Mexico residents in the most expedient time possible, generally no later than 45 calendar days after discovering a security breach. Statutory exceptions include certain risk determinations, and a law-enforcement delay can apply. — NMSA 1978, §§ 57-12C-6 and 57-12C-9

facts.label: Larger breaches
facts.value: When notification is required for more than 1,000 New Mexico residents following a single breach, the law also requires notification to the attorney general and major consumer reporting agencies. — NMSA 1978, § 57-12C-10

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in New Mexico
bullets: The New Mexico Department of Justice, headed by the attorney general, receives consumer complaints involving deceptive business practices.
Local police departments and county sheriffs receive reports of suspected criminal harassment; district attorneys prosecute state criminal cases.
New Mexico district courts hear civil claims, including defamation and requests for injunctive relief. Court jurisdiction and the relief requested determine the appropriate forum.

sections.heading: Common questions in New Mexico
bullets: Does AI involvement automatically make a post unlawful? No. Liability depends on the applicable claim or offense and its required elements.
Is every insulting message criminal harassment? No. Section 30-3A-2 requires a qualifying pattern, specified intent and the statutory emotional-distress standard.
Can deceptive advertising support a private lawsuit? Yes, when the Unfair Practices Act’s requirements are met, including qualifying monetary or property loss for damages.
Is a data breach notice always due immediately? No. The law requires notice as expeditiously as possible and generally within 45 calendar days, subject to statutory exceptions and delays.

ai-tech-law/new-york/deepfake-laws.summary: New York addresses deepfakes through several laws rather than one general ban on AI-generated content: Civil Rights Law § 52-c covers certain nonconsensual, digitally fabricated sexual depictions, while Penal Law § 245.15 criminalizes qualifying dissemination of intimate images, including images created or altered by digitization. Separate civil protections address intimate-image distribution and certain commercial uses of deceased personalities’ identities or deceased performers’ digital replicas, so liability depends on the content, consent, use, and statutory requirements.

facts.label: Civil claim for fabricated sexual depictions
facts.value: Civil Rights Law § 52-c gives a depicted individual a civil cause of action for qualifying unauthorized dissemination or publication of a sexually explicit depiction produced through digitization. It addresses depictions that make someone appear to give a performance they did not actually perform, including performances altered through digitization. — N.Y. Civil Rights Law § 52-c

facts.label: Consent and labeling
facts.value: The statute contains specific consent requirements. A disclaimer stating that a sexually explicit depiction was unauthorized, or that the depicted individual did not participate in its creation or development, does not by itself prevent liability. — N.Y. Civil Rights Law § 52-c

facts.label: Criminal coverage
facts.value: Unlawful dissemination or publication of an intimate image is a class A misdemeanor. The offense expressly reaches qualifying images created or altered by digitization, but requires proof of the statute’s elements, including intent to cause harm to another person’s emotional, financial, or physical welfare. — N.Y. Penal Law § 245.15

sections.heading: Which New York law covers which conduct?

rows: Unauthorized dissemination or publication of qualifying digitally fabricated sexual depictions.
Provides a private civil claim; it is not a general prohibition on synthetic media.
Qualifying nonconsensual dissemination or publication of intimate images, including digitized images.
Criminal liability requires the prosecution to establish the specified mental state and other elements.
Unlawful dissemination or publication of intimate images.
Provides civil remedies distinct from a criminal prosecution.
Certain commercial uses of deceased personalities’ identities and certain digital replicas of deceased performers.
Contains eligibility requirements, exceptions, and a 40-year post-death protection period.

facts.label: Not every deepfake is unlawful
facts.value: These provisions regulate defined conduct rather than AI generation in the abstract. Section 52-c includes exceptions concerning specified matters such as legitimate public concern, newsworthy material, and commentary or criticism; sexually explicit content is not automatically newsworthy merely because the depicted person is a public figure. — N.Y. Civil Rights Law § 52-c

facts.label: Civil relief
facts.value: Section 52-c authorizes monetary and injunctive relief, including compensatory damages, punitive damages, and reasonable attorney’s fees and costs. An injunction is a court order restricting conduct; it is separate from any criminal punishment. — N.Y. Civil Rights Law § 52-c

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in New York
bullets: New York State Supreme Court is the state’s general trial court and handles civil actions seeking damages and injunctive relief under these provisions.

Local police departments and county district attorneys handle complaints and prosecutions involving alleged violations of Penal Law § 245.15. A criminal complaint and a private civil lawsuit are separate proceedings.

sections.heading: Common questions in New York
bullets: Must a sexual deepfake show a real sexual event? No. Civil Rights Law § 52-c specifically addresses qualifying performances fabricated or altered through digitization.
Does labeling a sexual deepfake as fake eliminate liability? No. Section 52-c expressly limits the effect of disclaimers.
Is every AI impersonation a crime? No. Penal Law § 245.15 concerns specified intimate-image conduct, not every synthetic voice, photograph, or video.
Can protection continue after someone dies? Yes. Civil Rights Law § 50-f protects qualifying deceased personalities and performers, subject to its scope, exceptions, and time limit.

ai-tech-law/nevada/social-media-legal-is.summary: Nevada addresses social media disputes through online privacy rules, rights of publicity, defamation law and protections for certain speech connected to public issues, rather than through one comprehensive social media statute. Businesses operating covered websites or online services have specific privacy obligations, while commercial use of someone’s identity can require consent. AI-generated content is not automatically outside these laws, but liability depends on the particular conduct and the requirements of the applicable statute.

sections.heading: Nevada rules affecting social media and AI content

facts.label: Online privacy coverage
facts.value: Nevada’s online privacy provisions apply to qualifying operators of commercial websites and online services that collect covered information from Nevada consumers. The statutory definitions and exclusions matter; these provisions do not govern every account holder or every use of personal information. — NRS 603A.300–603A.360

facts.label: Commercial use of identity
facts.value: Nevada recognizes a right of publicity in a person’s name, voice, signature, photograph and likeness. Commercial use generally requires written consent, subject to statutory exceptions. An AI label does not itself supply that consent. — NRS 597.770–597.810

facts.label: Publicity exceptions
facts.value: Nevada provides exceptions for specified uses, including news, public affairs and sports broadcasts or publications. Whether a social media post qualifies depends on its use and context, not simply on whether it appears online. — NRS 597.790

facts.label: Protected speech and anti-SLAPP
facts.value: Nevada provides a special motion to dismiss certain claims based on good-faith communications furthering petition or free-speech rights in direct connection with an issue of public concern. The statute defines qualifying communications; it does not protect every social media statement. — NRS 41.637 and 41.660

rows: Covered operators must make a notice available identifying categories of information collected and categories of third parties with whom information may be shared, among other required disclosures.
Covered operators generally must respond to a verified opt-out request within 60 days. A necessary extension of up to 30 additional days requires notice to the consumer.
The Attorney General may seek an injunction or a civil penalty of up to $5,000 for each violation. These online privacy provisions do not establish a private right of action.
Available remedies include an injunction, actual damages of at least $750 and, where authorized, punitive damages and attorney’s fees.
A special motion generally must be filed within 60 days after service of the complaint; the court may allow a later filing for good cause.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Nevada
bullets: Nevada Attorney General, Bureau of Consumer Protection: receives consumer complaints, including complaints involving businesses’ privacy practices. Enforcement authority for the online privacy provisions appears in NRS 603A.360.
Nevada state courts: hear civil disputes involving unauthorized commercial use of identity and allegedly defamatory social media statements, subject to jurisdiction and venue requirements.
The court hearing the underlying civil lawsuit: decides a Nevada anti-SLAPP special motion and associated requests for statutory relief under NRS 41.660–41.670.

sections.heading: Common questions in Nevada
bullets: Does Nevada require deletion of all social media information on request? The online privacy provisions discussed here establish a qualified sale opt-out, not a general right to erase every post or account record.
Does every transfer of personal information count as a sale? No. Nevada uses a specific statutory definition involving monetary consideration and includes exclusions. — NRS 603A.333
Can an AI-generated voice raise publicity issues? Yes. Voice is expressly protected, although a claim still depends on commercial use and applicable exceptions. — NRS 597.770–597.790
Does anti-SLAPP protection cover knowingly false posts? The statutory definition of a good-faith communication requires truthfulness or absence of knowledge of falsehood. — NRS 41.637

ai-tech-law/north-dakota/terms-of-servic.summary: North Dakota applies its general contract rules to terms of service for AI products; electronic presentation does not, by itself, make those terms unenforceable. Enforceability depends on requirements including consent, a lawful purpose, and sufficient consideration, while state law limits contractual attempts to excuse certain misconduct. North Dakota’s electronic-transactions law recognizes electronic contracts and automated contracting, but it does not eliminate the underlying requirements for a valid agreement or override applicable consumer-protection law.

sections.heading: Contract requirements for AI terms of service

facts.label: Essential elements
facts.value: A North Dakota contract requires parties capable of contracting, their consent, a lawful object, and sufficient cause or consideration. These requirements apply when an AI provider seeks to enforce subscription terms, account rules, or other contractual conditions. — N.D.C.C. § 9-01-02

facts.label: Electronic form
facts.value: A record or signature cannot be denied legal effect or enforceability solely because it is electronic. A contract likewise cannot be denied effect solely because an electronic record was used in its formation. This prevents an electronic-format objection; it does not establish that every posted term became part of a contract. — N.D.C.C. § 9-16-07

facts.label: Agreement to transact electronically
facts.value: The Uniform Electronic Transactions Act applies to transactions between parties that have agreed to conduct transactions electronically. Whether they agreed is determined from the context and surrounding circumstances, including their conduct. — N.D.C.C. § 9-16-05

sections.heading: How state rules affect common AI contract provisions

rows: Electronic contracting is recognized, but the ordinary requirement of consent remains.
Electronic agents can form a contract even if no individual reviewed their actions or the resulting terms.
Contracts intended to exempt someone from responsibility for their own fraud, willful injury, or violation of law are against public policy.
Deceptive acts, false promises, and misrepresentations connected with selling or advertising merchandise are prohibited; merchandise includes services.

facts.label: Human review is not always required
facts.value: The electronic-transactions statute expressly addresses contracts formed through interactions between electronic agents. It also addresses interactions between an electronic agent and an individual who performs actions the individual is free to refuse and knows, or has reason to know, will complete a transaction. — N.D.C.C. § 9-16-14

facts.label: Consumer-fraud prohibition
facts.value: The consumer-fraud statute covers deceptive practices connected with the sale or advertisement of merchandise. Its prohibition applies whether or not anyone has actually been misled, deceived, or damaged; that does not mean every private claim succeeds without proof of injury. — N.D.C.C. § 51-15-02

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in North Dakota
bullets: The North Dakota Attorney General’s Consumer Protection Division receives consumer complaints involving allegedly deceptive business practices, including complaints about services.
North Dakota district courts hear civil contract disputes within their jurisdiction. A contract-enforcement lawsuit and an Attorney General consumer complaint are different proceedings.

sections.heading: Common questions in North Dakota
bullets: Are AI terms invalid because they are electronic? No. Electronic form alone is not a basis for denying enforceability under N.D.C.C. § 9-16-07.
Does posting terms establish consent? Posting alone does not establish all essential contract elements. Consent remains required under N.D.C.C. § 9-01-02.
Can software form a contract without human review? Yes. N.D.C.C. § 9-16-14 expressly recognizes specified automated transactions.
Can terms excuse the provider’s own fraud? A contract intended to exempt a party from responsibility for its own fraud is against public policy under N.D.C.C. § 9-08-02.

ai-tech-law/north-carolina/right-to-repa.summary: In North Carolina, repair disputes involving AI-enabled devices can implicate sales warranties, service contracts, federal warranty protections, and the state’s unfair or deceptive trade practices law. These laws can address defective products, broken repair promises, and certain warranty restrictions, but they do not themselves give every owner a general entitlement to source code, diagnostic software, replacement parts, or continued cloud access. The distinction between a purchased device and a separately supplied digital service matters.

sections.heading: North Carolina laws affecting repair rights

facts.label: Merchantability
facts.value: Unless properly excluded or modified, a merchant selling goods supplies an implied warranty that they are fit for their ordinary purposes. For an AI-enabled physical product, a repair dispute may therefore involve whether the product works as ordinary buyers would expect — N.C. Gen. Stat. § 25-2-314.

facts.label: Written and advertised promises
facts.value: A seller’s factual promises or product descriptions can create express warranties when they become part of the basis of the bargain. Formal words such as “warranty” are unnecessary, but statements of opinion or mere commendation do not create warranties — N.C. Gen. Stat. § 25-2-313.

facts.label: Independent repair and warranties
facts.value: For covered consumer-product warranties, federal law generally prohibits conditioning warranty coverage on branded parts or services unless they are supplied without charge or the Federal Trade Commission grants a waiver. Coverage can still exclude damage caused by outside parts or service — 15 U.S.C. § 2302(c); 16 C.F.R. § 700.10.

facts.label: Deceptive repair practices
facts.value: North Carolina prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce. Misleading repair representations can implicate this law, but an unsuccessful repair or warranty disagreement does not automatically establish a violation — N.C. Gen. Stat. § 75-1.1.

rows: Generally four years after accrual; the original agreement may reduce the period to no less than one year but cannot extend it.
Generally starts at tender of delivery, even if the defect is unknown; a limited exception applies to warranties explicitly extending to future performance.
After accepting goods, the buyer must notify the seller within a reasonable time after discovering, or when the buyer should have discovered, the breach.
An action under Chapter 75 is generally subject to a four-year limitation period after accrual.
Damages assessed for a qualifying Chapter 75 violation are trebled; attorney fees are discretionary under separate statutory conditions.

facts.label: Devices versus digital services
facts.value: North Carolina’s Uniform Commercial Code sales provisions apply to transactions in goods. Whether a software, cloud-access, or mixed hardware-service dispute falls within those provisions depends on the transaction; the presence of AI alone does not answer that question — N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 25-2-102, 25-2-105.

facts.label: Repair-only remedies
facts.value: A sales agreement may limit remedies to repair or replacement. If that limited remedy fails of its essential purpose, remedies otherwise available under the sales article may become available. This is not itself a general source-code disclosure requirement — N.C. Gen. Stat. § 25-2-719.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in North Carolina
bullets: The North Carolina Department of Justice’s Consumer Protection Division receives consumer complaints, including product, warranty, and repair disputes.

Private warranty and damages claims may proceed in North Carolina state trial courts. The proper court depends on jurisdiction and the relief sought; a consumer complaint to an agency is not a court action.

sections.heading: Common questions in North Carolina
bullets: Does an independent repair automatically void the warranty? No. Federal warranty rules distinguish prohibited branded-service conditions from exclusions for damage actually caused by outside work.
Must a manufacturer release an AI model or source code? The warranty and consumer-protection provisions discussed here do not establish that general entitlement.
Does every failed repair justify triple damages? No. Treble damages require a qualifying Chapter 75 claim, not merely dissatisfaction with a repair.
Can a warranty restrict the remedy to repair? Yes, subject to statutory limits, including the rule for a remedy that fails of its essential purpose.

ai-tech-law/tennessee/terms-of-service-e.summary: In Tennessee, an AI service’s terms of service can form an enforceable contract, but electronic presentation alone does not establish that a user agreed to every provision. Tennessee’s Uniform Electronic Transactions Act recognizes electronic contracts and signatures, while ordinary contract requirements and defenses still apply. Arbitration provisions may also be enforceable under federal or state law, and consumer-facing AI businesses remain subject to Tennessee’s prohibitions on unfair or deceptive practices despite using contractual disclaimers.

facts.label: Electronic form is legally recognized
facts.value: A record or signature cannot be denied legal effect solely because it is electronic. A contract likewise cannot be denied legal effect solely because an electronic record was used in its formation. This removes a paper-signature barrier; it does not automatically validate an AI provider’s terms — Tennessee Uniform Electronic Transactions Act, Tenn. Code Ann. § 47-10-107.

facts.label: Agreement to transact electronically
facts.value: The Act applies to transactions between parties who have agreed to conduct transactions electronically. Whether they agreed is determined from the context and surrounding circumstances, including their conduct — Tenn. Code Ann. § 47-10-105(b).

facts.label: Attributing a click or signature
facts.value: An electronic record or signature is attributable to a person if it was that person’s act. Its legal effect depends on the context and surrounding circumstances, including the parties’ agreement; attribution and enforceability are therefore distinct questions — Tenn. Code Ann. § 47-10-109.

sections.heading: Rules relevant to AI platform terms

columns: Tennessee rule or applicable federal rule
rows: Electronic agents can form a contract even when no individual reviewed their actions or the resulting terms — Tenn. Code Ann. § 47-10-114.

Written arbitration provisions in contracts involving commerce are generally enforceable, subject to generally applicable contract defenses and statutory exceptions — Federal Arbitration Act, 9 U.S.C. § 2.
Tennessee’s Uniform Arbitration Act recognizes qualifying written arbitration agreements, subject to grounds for revoking any contract — Tenn. Code Ann. § 29-5-302.

Representing that services have characteristics, uses, or benefits they do not have is an enumerated unlawful practice. That rule can matter when an AI provider markets capabilities its service lacks — Tenn. Code Ann. § 47-18-104(b)(5).
A waiver of the Tennessee Consumer Protection Act’s provisions is contrary to public policy, void, and unenforceable — Tenn. Code Ann. § 47-18-113(a).

facts.label: Private claim requirements
facts.value: A person suffering an ascertainable loss from an unlawful practice covered by the private-action provision may seek actual damages. An objectionable term alone does not establish the required loss or causation — Tenn. Code Ann. § 47-18-109(a)(1).

facts.label: Additional remedies
facts.value: For a willful or knowing violation, a court may award three times actual damages and other necessary and proper relief. The statute also permits reasonable attorney’s fees and costs upon a qualifying finding of a violation — Tenn. Code Ann. § 47-18-109(a)(3), (e)(1).

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Tennessee
bullets: The Tennessee Attorney General’s Division of Consumer Affairs accepts consumer complaints concerning businesses. Its complaint process is separate from a private lawsuit and does not make the office the consumer’s private lawyer.

Tennessee circuit and chancery courts are authorized forums for private actions under Tenn. Code Ann. § 47-18-109(a)(1). Whether a particular dispute must instead proceed in arbitration depends on the agreement and applicable law.

sections.heading: Common questions in Tennessee
bullets: Does an electronic signature make every term enforceable? No. Section 47-10-107 recognizes electronic form; it does not eliminate other contract requirements or defenses.
Can an automated AI transaction create a contract? Yes. Section 47-10-114 recognizes contract formation involving electronic agents.
Can terms waive Tennessee consumer-protection law? A waiver of the Act’s provisions is unenforceable under § 47-18-113(a).
Does every deceptive-practice allegation support a private lawsuit? No. The catchall prohibition in § 47-18-104(b)(27) is enforceable exclusively by the Attorney General.

ai-tech-law/wyoming/deepfake-laws.summary: In Wyoming, an AI-generated impersonation can raise legal issues under identity-theft, stalking, consumer-protection, or defamation law, depending on how it is created and used. These laws do not make every synthetic image, cloned voice, or fabricated video unlawful: the relevant questions include intent, use of identifying information, consumer deception, repeated harassment, and injury to reputation. A deepfake’s realistic appearance alone does not establish the elements of any particular claim or crime.

sections.heading: Wyoming laws relevant to deepfake misuse

facts.label: Identity theft
facts.value: Wyoming prohibits obtaining another person’s personal identifying information and using it, without that person’s consent, to obtain goods, services, property, or another thing of value, or to commit a crime. A cloned voice or fabricated likeness used in an impersonation scheme must still satisfy the statute’s identifying-information and prohibited-use requirements. — Wyo. Stat. § 6-3-901

facts.label: Stalking
facts.value: Stalking requires intent to harass and a course of conduct reasonably likely to harass another person. Wyoming’s definition of a course of conduct involves a series of acts evidencing continuity of purpose; it excludes constitutionally protected activity. Repeated deepfake-related harassment may therefore present a different legal question from a single publication. — Wyo. Stat. § 6-2-506

facts.label: Deceptive business practices
facts.value: The Wyoming Consumer Protection Act identifies prohibited deceptive practices committed knowingly in the course of business and in connection with a consumer transaction. Its provisions include specified misrepresentations about sponsorship, approval, affiliation, and goods or services—issues potentially implicated by fabricated endorsements. — Wyo. Stat. §§ 40-12-101–40-12-114, particularly § 40-12-105

sections.heading: How the use of a deepfake affects the legal analysis

rows: Impersonation used to obtain money or services
Unauthorized identifying-information use and a statutory prohibited purpose must be established.
Repeated targeted distribution intended to harass
The statute requires intent and a qualifying course of conduct; protected expression is excluded.
Fabricated endorsement in a consumer transaction
The business, consumer-transaction, knowledge, and particular deceptive-practice requirements matter.
Wyoming generally provides a one-year limitation period for libel or slander, measured from accrual. — § 1-3-105

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Wyoming
bullets: The Wyoming Attorney General’s Consumer Protection and Antitrust Unit handles consumer-protection matters, including complaints about allegedly deceptive business practices. This is not a general forum for every offensive or misleading AI-generated post.

Local police departments and county sheriffs receive reports of suspected crimes. County and prosecuting attorneys handle state criminal prosecutions; a private complainant does not independently prosecute a criminal case.
Wyoming state courts hear civil claims within their jurisdiction. The appropriate court depends on the claim and requested relief, rather than simply on whether AI technology was involved.

sections.heading: Common questions in Wyoming
bullets: Does a convincing AI impersonation automatically establish identity theft? No. Section 6-3-901 requires the identifying-information, lack-of-consent, and prohibited-use elements; resemblance alone does not establish them.

Can a fake endorsement raise consumer-protection issues? Yes. Knowing misrepresentations about sponsorship, approval, or affiliation in a business-related consumer transaction can implicate § 40-12-105.
Is every offensive deepfake stalking? No. Section 6-2-506 requires intent to harass and a qualifying course of conduct, and excludes constitutionally protected activity.

What deadline matters for a reputational claim? Wyoming’s limitation statute generally gives libel or slander claims one year from accrual. Whether a particular publication supports such a claim is a separate question; talk to a lawyer.

ai-tech-law/texas/right-to-repair.summary: In Texas, disputes over repairing AI-enabled devices can involve consumer-protection law, warranty restrictions, software contracts, and personal-data rights rather than a single legal rule. The Texas Deceptive Trade Practices–Consumer Protection Act addresses misleading repair and warranty representations, while federal warranty law limits certain restrictions on independent repairs; Texas privacy rights concern personal data and do not themselves require manufacturers to release repair tools, source code, or AI model weights.

facts.label: Misleading repair representations
facts.value: The Deceptive Trade Practices–Consumer Protection Act prohibits representing that goods or services have characteristics, uses, or benefits they do not have. It also prohibits falsely representing that an agreement confers or involves particular rights, remedies, or obligations. These provisions can apply to statements about repair services or warranty coverage. — Texas Business & Commerce Code § 17.46(b)(5), (12).

facts.label: Consumer claims
facts.value: A qualifying consumer may seek relief when a listed deceptive practice, relied on to the consumer’s detriment, is a producing cause of economic damages or mental anguish damages. Breach of an express or implied warranty is another statutory basis for a claim. Not every unsuccessful repair establishes a violation. — Texas Business & Commerce Code § 17.50(a).

facts.label: Independent repair and warranties
facts.value: For covered consumer products, a warrantor generally cannot condition a written or implied warranty on using a branded article or service unless it is provided without charge or the Federal Trade Commission grants a waiver. This does not require coverage for damage actually caused by an independent repair. — 15 U.S.C. § 2302(c); 16 C.F.R. § 700.10.

rows: Generally two years after the deceptive act occurred or was discovered, or reasonably should have been discovered.
Generally written notice at least 60 days before suit; statutory exceptions apply.
Civil jurisdiction generally extends to $20,000, excluding statutory interest and court costs, subject to jurisdictional exceptions.
Covered controllers generally have 45 days, with a possible additional 45 days when reasonably necessary and timely explained.
Access, correction, deletion, and portability rights do not themselves create an entitlement to diagnostic tools or proprietary AI technology.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Texas
bullets: Texas Office of the Attorney General, Consumer Protection Division: receives complaints about deceptive business practices, including repair and warranty disputes. An agency complaint is separate from a consumer’s civil lawsuit.
Texas Office of the Attorney General: enforces the Texas Data Privacy and Security Act. Chapter 541 does not create a private right of action for violations.

Texas justice courts: hear qualifying civil claims within their jurisdiction. Other repair-related civil claims may belong in county or district court, depending on the claim, amount, and applicable jurisdictional statutes.
Federal Trade Commission: receives reports about potentially unlawful warranty restrictions involving consumer products.

sections.heading: Common questions in Texas
bullets: Does buying an AI device automatically provide access to its source code? No. The consumer-protection, warranty, and privacy provisions described here do not themselves grant that access.
Can a manufacturer exclude damage caused by an independent repair? Yes. Federal restrictions on warranty tying do not require a manufacturer to cover damage caused by unauthorized parts or service.

Does a Texas privacy request provide every file stored by a device maker? No. Chapter 541 concerns specified rights in personal data and includes limitations and exemptions; it is not a general disclosure law for proprietary technology.

Does a failed repair automatically establish a DTPA claim? No. The applicable statutory elements must be established, including consumer status and the required connection between actionable conduct and injury.

ai-tech-law/virginia/deepfake-laws.summary: Virginia’s intimate-image law expressly reaches manipulated images that depict a recognizable real person, making some sexually explicit deepfakes a criminal offense even when the depicted nudity never occurred. Liability depends on the statute’s requirements, including malicious dissemination or sale, intent to coerce, harass, or intimidate, and knowledge that distribution is unauthorized; separate Virginia statutes provide civil remedies for prohibited intimate-image distribution and certain unauthorized uses of someone’s identity.

sections.heading: Virginia’s criminal rule for intimate deepfakes

facts.label: Main statute
facts.value: Virginia Code § 18.2-386.2 prohibits malicious dissemination or sale of specified nude or undressed images with intent to coerce, harass, or intimidate, when the distributor knows or has reason to know distribution is unauthorized. The statute covers images created by any means whatsoever. — Va. Code § 18.2-386.2.

facts.label: Recognizable real people
facts.value: The definition of another person includes someone whose image was used to create, adapt, or modify an image intended to depict an actual person who is recognizable by face, likeness, or another distinguishing characteristic. This language expressly addresses manipulated depictions. — Va. Code § 18.2-386.2.

facts.label: Covered exposure
facts.value: The image must depict total nudity or undress exposing the genitals, pubic area, buttocks, or female breast. An AI-generated image is not automatically prohibited simply because it is synthetic or misleading. — Va. Code § 18.2-386.2.

facts.label: Criminal penalty
facts.value: A violation is a Class 1 misdemeanor, punishable by confinement in jail for up to 12 months, a fine of up to $2,500, or both. — Va. Code §§ 18.2-386.2 and 18.2-11.

rows: Can fall within the criminal statute when the depicted person is recognizable and the distribution, intent, and knowledge requirements are satisfied. — § 18.2-386.2.
Creating an image without distributing it
Creation alone is not the dissemination or sale prohibited by this particular provision. — § 18.2-386.2.
Civil claim for prohibited intimate-image distribution
A person depicted in an image distributed in violation of § 18.2-386.2 has a civil cause of action against the person who disseminated or sold it. — § 8.01-40.4.

Use of a person’s name, portrait, or picture for advertising or trade without the required written consent can support an action to stop the use and recover damages. Application to a particular synthetic depiction depends on the facts. — § 8.01-40.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Virginia
bullets: Local police departments and county sheriffs receive reports of suspected criminal intimate-image distribution. The local Commonwealth’s Attorney handles prosecution of Virginia criminal offenses.

General district courts ordinarily hear adult Class 1 misdemeanor prosecutions, including charges under § 18.2-386.2; juvenile and domestic relations district court jurisdiction can apply in specified circumstances.
Virginia state courts hear civil claims under § 8.01-40.4. The appropriate court depends on jurisdiction and the relief requested.
Virginia Code § 8.01-40 expressly provides for an action in circuit court over qualifying unauthorized advertising or trade uses of a person’s name, portrait, or picture.

sections.heading: Common questions in Virginia
bullets: Must the nudity be authentic? No. Section 18.2-386.2 expressly includes qualifying created or modified depictions of recognizable actual people.
Is every deceptive deepfake covered by this criminal law? No. Section 18.2-386.2 addresses specified nude or undressed images and requires the statutory intent, knowledge, and distribution elements.
Does permission to make an image necessarily authorize sharing it? No. The statute addresses whether dissemination or sale is licensed or authorized.
Can the depicted person bring a lawsuit? Yes. Section 8.01-40.4 provides a civil cause of action for dissemination or sale violating § 18.2-386.2.
