ai-tech-law/rhode-island/social-media-le.summary: Rhode Island social media disputes can involve statutory privacy rights, unauthorized commercial use of a person’s name or image, and consumer data protections, including when AI tools generate or distribute the content. The Rhode Island Data Transparency and Privacy Protection Act took effect January 1, 2026, but its coverage and exemptions matter: an offensive post, an AI-generated likeness, and a platform’s collection of personal data raise different legal questions rather than falling under one general social media law.

sections.heading: Privacy and AI-generated social media content

facts.label: Four protected privacy interests
facts.value: Rhode Island expressly recognizes protection against unreasonable intrusion upon physical solitude or seclusion, appropriation of a name or likeness, unreasonable publicity given to private life, and publicity that unreasonably places someone in a false light. Each claim has its own statutory requirements; objectionable online content does not automatically establish liability. — R.I. Gen. Laws § 9-1-28.1.

facts.label: Unauthorized commercial use
facts.value: A person whose name, portrait, or picture is used within Rhode Island for advertising or trade purposes without written consent may seek an injunction and damages. The statute includes exceptions, so the distinction between an advertisement and other expression matters. — R.I. Gen. Laws § 9-1-28.

facts.label: AI does not replace the legal elements
facts.value: For an AI-generated social post, the relevant questions can include whether it appropriates an identifiable person’s likeness, falsely portrays that person, or publicizes private facts. These Rhode Island statutes address the underlying conduct rather than establishing that every synthetic image or inaccurate AI output is unlawful. — R.I. Gen. Laws §§ 9-1-28 and 9-1-28.1.

sections.heading: How common online disputes fit Rhode Island law

rows: Unauthorized advertising or trade use may implicate § 9-1-28; appropriation may also implicate § 9-1-28.1.
The statutory false-light right may be relevant, but its publicity and other requirements must be established. § 9-1-28.1.
Unreasonable publicity given to private life is a recognized privacy claim. § 9-1-28.1.
Unreasonable intrusion upon physical solitude or seclusion is separately protected. § 9-1-28.1.
Covered personal-data processing may trigger consumer rights under the Data Transparency and Privacy Protection Act. Chapter 6-48.1.

facts.label: Scope and rights
facts.value: The Rhode Island Data Transparency and Privacy Protection Act establishes rights for consumers concerning covered processing of personal data, including access, correction, deletion, portability, and specified opt-outs. Coverage depends on statutory applicability rules and exemptions; these rights are not a universal removal mechanism for every social media post. — R.I. Gen. Laws ch. 6-48.1.

facts.label: Enforcement
facts.value: The attorney general has exclusive authority to enforce the Act. The Act does not create a private right of action, which distinguishes its enforcement process from civil claims under Rhode Island’s privacy statutes. — R.I. Gen. Laws ch. 6-48.1.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Rhode Island
bullets: Rhode Island Office of the Attorney General: the state enforcement authority for the Data Transparency and Privacy Protection Act.

Rhode Island civil courts: claims under §§ 9-1-28 and 9-1-28.1 are distinct from attorney general enforcement of the data statute. The appropriate court depends on jurisdiction and the relief requested.
For questions about overlapping privacy claims, speech protections, or jurisdiction, talk to a lawyer.

sections.heading: Common questions in Rhode Island
bullets: Is every AI deepfake unlawful? No. Liability under these statutes depends on the particular use and the elements of the applicable claim.
Does Rhode Island recognize false-light privacy claims? Yes. Section 9-1-28.1 expressly recognizes that privacy interest.
Can someone sue under the new consumer data Act? The Act itself provides no private right of action; enforcement belongs to the attorney general.
Can an unauthorized advertisement using someone’s picture lead to damages? Yes. Section 9-1-28 authorizes damages and injunctive relief when its requirements are met.

ai-tech-law/texas/deepfake-laws.summary: Texas regulates deepfakes through targeted laws, including an election offense and a criminal provision addressing sexually explicit deepfake material, rather than treating every AI-generated depiction as unlawful. Election Code Section 255.004 covers deceptive videos created with the required election-related intent and published or distributed within 30 days of an election; Penal Code Section 21.165 separately addresses sexually explicit deepfakes, where consent and the statutory elements matter. Whether either provision applies depends on the material and the conduct involved.

facts.label: Conduct covered
facts.value: The election offense applies when a person, with intent to injure a candidate or influence an election’s result, creates a deepfake video and causes it to be published or distributed within 30 days of an election. Creating the video and causing its publication or distribution are both parts of the statutory test. — Texas Election Code § 255.004(b)

facts.label: Definition
facts.value: A deepfake video is a video created with intent to deceive that appears to depict a real person performing an action that did not occur in reality. The definition focuses on deceptive depiction, not a particular AI product, model, or editing technique. — Texas Election Code § 255.004(d)

facts.label: Criminal classification
facts.value: An offense under Section 255.004 is a Class A misdemeanor. Texas’s general punishment range for that classification is a fine of up to $4,000, confinement in jail for up to one year, or both. — Texas Election Code § 255.004(c); Texas Penal Code § 12.21

rows: Potentially covered when the creation, intent, publication or distribution, and timing elements are satisfied. — Election Code § 255.004(b)
Texas has a separate criminal provision addressing unlawful production or distribution of sexually explicit deepfake material; it is not limited to elections. — Penal Code § 21.165
The election deepfake definition expressly concerns video. Audio-only content does not meet that definition merely because it imitates someone’s voice. — Election Code § 255.004(d)

The 30-day requirement concerns publication or distribution before an election. It is an element of this offense, not a general deadline for reporting all deepfake conduct. — Election Code § 255.004(b)(2)

Synthetic production alone does not establish the election offense: the statutory definition requires intent to deceive, and the offense requires additional election-related elements. — Election Code § 255.004(b), (d)

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Texas
bullets: Local police departments and county sheriffs receive reports of suspected criminal conduct, including conduct potentially covered by the election and sexually explicit deepfake statutes.
Criminal charges are pursued by the prosecuting authority with jurisdiction. A private complaint is not itself a criminal prosecution.
County-level criminal courts generally handle Class A misdemeanor prosecutions, including the election deepfake offense; the particular court depends on the county’s court structure.

The Texas Ethics Commission administers civil enforcement of specified political-advertising requirements, but its complaint process is distinct from criminal prosecution under Election Code Section 255.004.

sections.heading: Common questions in Texas
bullets: Is every deepfake illegal? No. Section 255.004 requires particular intent, conduct, and election timing; synthetic content alone does not establish that offense.

Does the election statute require proof that voters changed their votes? Its stated elements require intent to injure a candidate or influence an election, not proof that the election result actually changed.
Does the 30-day election rule govern sexual deepfakes? No. Penal Code Section 21.165 is a separate provision and does not use that election window.

Can an authentic recording be a deepfake under this definition? A recording accurately depicting an action that actually occurred does not meet the statutory requirement that the depicted action did not occur in reality.

ai-tech-law/washington/data-privacy-righ.summary: Washington’s My Health My Data Act protects consumer health data outside traditional medical-record settings, including certain health information inferred by algorithms or machine learning, and gives covered consumers access, deletion, and consent-withdrawal rights. Washington also regulates commercial biometric identifiers and requires notices for qualifying data breaches, but these laws have different coverage and enforcement rules; they do not create a general right to inspect every AI system or delete every kind of personal information.

facts.label: Coverage
facts.value: The My Health My Data Act covers Washington residents and individuals whose consumer health data is collected in Washington. Its consumer definition excludes individuals acting in an employment context. Covered businesses include entities doing business in Washington or targeting products or services to Washington consumers, subject to statutory exclusions. — RCW 19.373.010

facts.label: AI-generated health inferences
facts.value: Consumer health data includes identifiable information about physical or mental health and certain information derived or extrapolated from nonhealth information through algorithms or machine learning. An inference can therefore be protected even when the person never supplied a medical record. — RCW 19.373.010

facts.label: Exemptions
facts.value: The Act excludes specified information governed by other laws, including HIPAA protected health information and health care information collected, used, or disclosed under Washington’s Uniform Health Care Information Act. It is not a replacement for those medical-privacy laws. — RCW 19.373.100

rows: Consumers may confirm collection, sharing, or sale and access their health data, including a list of third parties and affiliates receiving it.
Consumers may withdraw consent for collection and sharing of consumer health data.
Consumers may request deletion; the business must also notify relevant affiliates, processors, contractors, and other recipients to delete the data.
Businesses generally must respond within 45 days. A reasonably necessary extension of another 45 days requires timely notice explaining the delay.
Consent is generally required unless necessary to provide a requested product or service. Sharing consent must be separate from collection consent.
Selling or offering to sell consumer health data requires a valid authorization separate from consent to collect or share.

facts.label: Commercial biometric identifiers
facts.value: Washington separately regulates enrollment and use of biometric identifiers for commercial purposes. Its definition includes fingerprints, voiceprints, and specified biological patterns used to identify a person; it excludes photographs, video or audio recordings, and data generated from them. — RCW 19.375.010–.020

facts.label: Security and retention
facts.value: Possessors of enrolled biometric identifiers must exercise reasonable care against unauthorized access or acquisition and may retain them no longer than reasonably necessary for authorized purposes specified by law. — RCW 19.375.020

facts.label: Breach notification
facts.value: For qualifying breaches involving covered persons or businesses, consumer notice is generally due without unreasonable delay and within 30 calendar days after discovery, subject to statutory exceptions. Breaches requiring notice to more than 500 Washington residents also require Attorney General notice. — RCW 19.255.010

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Washington
bullets: Washington Attorney General: accepts consumer complaints and enforces the My Health My Data Act through the Consumer Protection Act. — RCW 19.373.090

Washington courts: a private Consumer Protection Act action may be available for a My Health My Data violation when the required elements are established; a violation does not automatically establish damages. — RCW 19.373.090
Washington Attorney General: has exclusive enforcement authority under the separate commercial biometric-identifiers chapter. — RCW 19.375.030

sections.heading: Common questions in Washington
bullets: Can an AI health prediction be protected? Yes, qualifying identifiable health inferences fall within consumer health data. — RCW 19.373.010
Does HIPAA coverage determine everything? No. Washington’s Act reaches qualifying health data outside its medical-information exemptions. — RCW 19.373.100
Can a business refuse a request? The Act permits authentication requirements and provides an appeal process for refusals. — RCW 19.373.040

Are health-related geofences restricted? Yes. The Act prohibits specified tracking, collection, and messaging uses of geofences around entities providing in-person health care services. — RCW 19.373.080

ai-tech-law/oregon/social-media-legal-is.summary: Oregon regulates social media and AI-related practices through its consumer privacy law, restrictions on employer access to personal accounts, and consumer protection rules against deceptive business conduct. The Oregon Consumer Privacy Act gives eligible residents rights over covered personal data, including certain profiling and targeted advertising, but it does not cover every platform or every use of AI. Enforcement and available remedies depend on the particular law involved.

sections.heading: Oregon privacy rights affecting social media and AI

facts.label: Scope and coverage
facts.value: The Oregon Consumer Privacy Act applies to businesses and other entities meeting its coverage requirements, subject to statutory exemptions. A consumer is an Oregon resident acting outside a commercial or employment context, so employment records do not receive these consumer rights merely because they contain personal information. — ORS 646A.570–646A.589

facts.label: Access, correction and deletion
facts.value: Covered consumers can request confirmation of processing, access to personal data, correction of inaccuracies and deletion. They can also request a list of specific third parties to which the controller disclosed personal data, subject to the statute's terms. — ORS 646A.570–646A.589

facts.label: Request deadlines
facts.value: Controllers generally must respond to consumer rights requests within 45 days. A further 45-day extension is permitted when reasonably necessary, with notice and an explanation during the initial response period. The law also requires an appeal process for refusals. — ORS 646A.570–646A.589

facts.label: Enforcement
facts.value: The Oregon Attorney General enforces the privacy act and may seek civil penalties of up to $7,500 per violation. The act does not create a private right of action for consumers. — ORS 646A.570–646A.589

sections.heading: Rules for common social media and AI situations

rows: Targeted advertising or sale of personal data
Covered consumers have opt-out rights, subject to statutory definitions and exceptions.
The opt-out right reaches profiling used for decisions producing legal or similarly significant effects; it is not a general prohibition on AI recommendations.
Covered controllers generally need consent to process sensitive data, including specified health information and biometric data used for identification.
Employers generally cannot require workers or applicants to disclose credentials for personal social media accounts or compel access, subject to statutory exceptions.
False representations about goods or services can violate Oregon's Unlawful Trade Practices Act, whether the promotional content is human-written or AI-generated.

sections.heading: Where to file or complain in Oregon
bullets: The Oregon Department of Justice accepts consumer privacy complaints and enforces the Oregon Consumer Privacy Act.
The Oregon Department of Justice's consumer protection program receives complaints about deceptive business practices, including online marketing.
The Oregon Bureau of Labor and Industries handles complaints involving unlawful employment practices, including Oregon's personal social media account protections.
Oregon circuit courts hear qualifying civil claims under the Unlawful Trade Practices Act. Private claims require the statutory elements; they are distinct from privacy-act enforcement. — ORS 646.638

sections.heading: Common questions in Oregon
bullets: Can someone sue directly under Oregon's privacy act? No. The act assigns enforcement to the Attorney General and does not provide a private lawsuit under that act.
Can an employer demand a personal Instagram password? Generally no. ORS 659A.330 protects personal social media credentials, although statutory exceptions apply.
Does the privacy act cover every AI chatbot? No. Coverage depends on the entity, processing activity, statutory thresholds and exemptions—not simply whether a product uses AI.

Does deleting a platform account necessarily exercise every privacy right? No. Account closure and a statutory personal-data deletion request are different actions, and lawful retention exceptions may apply.
